This delay in gametogenesis onset allows for the substantial somatic growth required before an individual can contribute to the pack's breeding efforts.

In contrast to these adult masses, the wet weight at weaning is 2350 grams [Wwx = 2350 grams], representing a massive increase from the birth weight. This nearly tenfold increase in mass over the 58-day nursing period underscores the critical role of the dam's lactation and the provisioning efforts of the entire pack in supporting the rapid growth of the dependent young.

Maximum longevity for the dhole, based on records for captive individuals living under core body temperature conditions of 38.8 °C [T = 38.8 °C], is approximately 16.1 years [am = approximately 16.1 years]. This peak ingestion rate is necessary to sustain the high metabolic demands of a large, cursorial predator that often travels extensively across its home range.

The social structure of dhole packs plays a pivotal role in the survival and growth of offspring, as cooperative breeding extends beyond the mother to include multiple adult helpers from the pack.
